#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# demo.sh — launch the AO Adapter Proving Ground (or record it).
#
#   ./demo.sh              # interactive deck + stage
#   ./demo.sh --record     # same, captured to evalrig.cast with asciinema
#   ./demo.sh --record out.cast
#
# Works whether or not you're already inside Zellij:
#   - outside Zellij  -> starts a new Zellij session with the layout.
#   - inside Zellij   -> opens the demo as a new TAB in your current session
#                        (nesting a new session is what Zellij refuses).
#
# The deck (left) is `ao evalrig`; the stage (right) is a shell the deck drives
# to run the real `go test` for each cell. Quit the deck with `q`.
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"
backend="$repo/backend"

for bin in zellij go; do
    command -v "$bin" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "demo.sh: '$bin' not found in PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
done

echo "Building ao …"
( cd "$backend" && go build -o "$backend/bin/ao" ./cmd/ao )
ao_bin="$backend/bin/ao"

# A resolved layout with absolute paths. Panes inherit the Zellij *server*
# environment, not this script's, so a relative cwd or a PATH export here would
# not reach them — bake the absolute binary path and cwd into the layout.
layout="$here/.evalrig.local.kdl"
cat > "$layout" <<KDL
layout {
    cwd "$backend"
    pane split_direction="vertical" {
        pane name="deck" size="58%" command="$ao_bin" {
            args "evalrig"
        }
        pane name="stage" size="42%"
    }
}
KDL

record=0
cast="$here/evalrig.cast"
if [[ "${1:-}" == "--record" ]]; then
    record=1
    [[ -n "${2:-}" ]] && cast="$2"
fi

# Already inside Zellij: open a new tab rather than nesting a session.
if [[ -n "${ZELLIJ:-}" ]]; then
    if [[ "$record" == 1 ]]; then
        echo "Note: --record must run from OUTSIDE Zellij (asciinema needs to own the session)." >&2
        echo "Opening the demo in a new tab instead — record your terminal separately." >&2
    fi
    echo "Inside Zellij → opening the proving ground in a new tab (switch tabs to see it)."
    exec zellij action new-tab --layout "$layout" --name evalrig
fi

# Fresh terminal: start a new named session with the layout.
session="evalrig-$$"
if [[ "$record" == 1 ]]; then
    command -v asciinema >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "demo.sh: asciinema not found" >&2; exit 1; }
    echo "Recording to $cast …"
    exec asciinema rec --overwrite -c "zellij --session '$session' --layout '$layout'" "$cast"
fi
exec zellij --session "$session" --layout "$layout"

lines: # A resolved layout with absolute paths. Panes inherit the Zellij *server*
# environment, not this script's, so a relative cwd or a PATH export here would
-# not reach them — bake the absolute binary path and cwd into the layout.
+# not reach them — bake the absolute binary path and cwd into each pane. The
+# cwd MUST be per-pane: a new tab in an existing session inherits the session's
+# cwd, and a layout-level `cwd` does not override it (so the stage would land in
+# the repo root and `go test ./internal/...` would fail to find the module).

#!/usr/bin/env bash
#
# demo.sh — launch the AO Adapter Proving Ground: two panes side by side,
# deck (ao evalrig) on the left, stage (a shell the deck drives) on the right.
#
#   ./demo.sh
#
# Works inside or outside Zellij:
#   - inside Zellij  -> opens the demo as a new TAB (Zellij won't nest sessions).
#   - outside Zellij -> starts a new session.
#
# The two-pane layout is passed inline (no layout file is written). Each pane's
# cwd is the absolute backend dir so the stage runs `go test ./internal/...`
# regardless of where Zellij was started. Quit the deck with `q`.
#
# To record: run `vhs evalrig.tape` for a standalone GIF of the deck, or
# screen-record this two-pane session.
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"
backend="$repo/backend"

for bin in zellij go; do
    command -v "$bin" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "demo.sh: '$bin' not found in PATH" >&2; exit 1; }
done

echo "Building ao …"
( cd "$backend" && go build -o "$backend/bin/ao" ./cmd/ao )
ao_bin="$backend/bin/ao"

layout="layout {
    pane split_direction=\"vertical\" {
        pane name=\"deck\" size=\"58%\" cwd=\"$backend\" command=\"$ao_bin\" {
            args \"evalrig\"
        }
        pane name=\"stage\" size=\"42%\" cwd=\"$backend\"
    }
}"

if [[ -n "${ZELLIJ:-}" ]]; then
    echo "Inside Zellij → opening the proving ground in a new tab (switch tabs to see it)."
    exec zellij action new-tab --layout-string "$layout" --name evalrig
fi

exec zellij --session "evalrig-$$" --layout-string "$layout"

# AO Adapter Proving Ground

An interactive, recordable demonstration that every agent adapter is tested
along the six dimensions we verify by hand:

| # | Dimension | What it proves |
|---|-----------|----------------|
| 1 | **spawn** | the launch command is well-formed, deterministic, and matches the declared prompt-delivery strategy |
| 2 | **activity** | the hooks the adapter installs are actually dispatched (`ao hooks <tok>` has a deriver) |
| 3 | **sessioninfo** | title/summary/id are derived from metadata only — never by reading transcripts |
| 4 | **permissions** | `default` emits no flag; each non-default mode maps to a distinct, real flag |
| 5 | **hooks** | install is idempotent and writes a worktree-local (non-tracked) config |
| 6 | **commands** | the exact launch/restore argv, snapshotted for review against each agent's CLI docs |

The verdicts come from the in-process conformance engine in
`backend/internal/adapters/agent/conformance` — the *same code CI runs* — so the
demo and the regression guard can never disagree.

## The two surfaces

- **Control deck** (`ao evalrig`) — a Bubble Tea TUI rendering the
  adapters × dimensions matrix. The presenter runs cells one keypress at a time.
- **Stage** — a sibling Zellij pane the deck drives (via `zellij action paste`)
  to run the real `go test` for each selected cell, so an audience watches
  genuine PASS lines while the matrix cell fills in.

```
┌─ deck (ao evalrig) ───────────┬─ stage (go test live) ─────────┐
│ HARNESS     SPAWN ACT INFO …  │ $ go test … -run …/spawn -v    │
│ claude-code   ✓    ✓   ✓  …   │ === RUN   TestConformance/…     │
│▸opencode      ✓    ▲   ✓  …   │ --- PASS: …                     │
│ …                             │                                 │
└───────────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘
```

Legend: `✓` pass · `▲` gap (wired-but-broken) · `✗` fail (contract violation) ·
`–` n/a (adapter limitation) · `·` not run yet.

## Run it

```bash
# Interactive two-pane demo (Zellij). Requires: zellij, go.
test/evalrig/demo.sh
```

`demo.sh` works whether or not you're already inside Zellij: from a fresh
terminal it starts a new session; from inside an existing session it opens the
demo as a new **tab** (Zellij refuses to nest a new session). Either way it
generates a layout with absolute paths so the panes find `ao` and run `go test`
from `backend/` regardless of the inherited environment.

Keys: `enter` run+advance · `space`/`r` re-run · `a` run row · `A` run all ·
arrows / `hjkl` move · `q` quit.

Run the deck alone (matrix-only, no stage) from anywhere:

```bash
cd backend && go run ./cmd/ao evalrig
```

### Live mode (hybrid)

With a running daemon and a registered project, the deck can spawn a real agent
and watch its actual activity and session info:

```bash
ao start                                  # daemon
ao project add … && ao evalrig --project <project-id>
```

Press `L` on an adapter whose binary is installed: the deck spawns it via the
daemon and a live panel shows the real activity state
(`active → idle → waiting_input → exited`) and the hook-derived title as they
change. `x` stops watching. Adapters whose binary isn't installed stay
deterministic-only — the deck says so rather than failing.

## Record it

```bash
# Live, presenter-paced capture (terminal-native .cast). Requires: asciinema.
test/evalrig/demo.sh --record            # -> test/evalrig/evalrig.cast
asciinema play test/evalrig/evalrig.cast

# Deterministic, embeddable GIF trailer (matrix-only). Requires: vhs.
cd test/evalrig && vhs evalrig.tape      # -> evalrig.gif
```

Use **asciinema** to prove you drove it live at your own pace; use **VHS** to
regenerate a clean GIF for a README/Slack/PR. Both reuse the same deck — they're
recorders, not separate rigs.

## The engine underneath (run without the TUI)

```bash
cd backend

# The full matrix + per-cell detail, as text (report-only):
go test ./internal/adapters/agent/conformance/ -run TestConformance -v

# One cell:
go test ./internal/adapters/agent/conformance/ -run 'TestConformance/opencode/activity' -v

# Turn it into an enforcing CI gate (fail on FAIL/GAP and golden drift):
AOEVAL_STRICT=1 go test ./internal/adapters/agent/conformance/...

# Regenerate the golden command snapshots + matrix.txt after an intended change:
AOEVAL_UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/adapters/agent/conformance/...
```

Golden launch/restore commands live in
`backend/internal/adapters/agent/conformance/testdata/golden/<harness>.txt`.

## Adding a new adapter

A new harness is registered in one place —
`backend/internal/adapters/agent/registry` (`Constructors`) — and, if it reports
activity, mapped in `backend/internal/adapters/agent/activitydispatch`
(`Derivers`). The proving ground picks it up automatically; the conformance
suite will immediately show its row.

content.text:
You were right to push back — I'd been validating a single manual paste, not the keys you actually press. This time I reproduced it against the **real `ao evalrig` TUI** and verified the fix the same way.

## The bug (reproduced)

Pressing **`a`/`A`** fires every cell's check in its own goroutine; each typed `paste`+`Enter` into the stage, and they **interleaved** → `…-count=1go test…` → `invalid value "1go"`. I confirmed it by sending `a` to the real deck pane and seeing all six commands mashed on one line.

## The fix (verified against the real TUI)

1. **Serialized stage writes** — a mutex makes each `paste`+`Enter` atomic, so even rapid presses can't interleave.
2. **Only single-cell runs touch the stage** — `enter`/`space`/`r` show one test; `a`/`A` just fill the matrix in-process (no flood, no garble).

Then I drove the actual deck headlessly and checked the real stage:
- `a` (run row) → stage stays clean, **0** garbled lines
- single `enter` → exactly **1** clean command → `--- PASS: TestConformance/claude-code/spawn … ok …conformance`
- **3 rapid enters** → still **0** garbling

Plus a `-race` regression test (`TestStageSerializesConcurrentWrites`: 16 concurrent `Run`s produce perfectly paired paste→Enter, never two pastes in a row). Full build + lint + `-race` green.

## What you'll see now

```bash
test/evalrig/demo.sh
```

- **`enter`** on a cell → one real `go test … PASS` scrolls in the stage, cell flips.
- **`a` / `A`** → the matrix fills fast (verdicts are in-process); the stage isn't touched.

#
# demo.sh — launch the AO Adapter Proving Ground: two panes side by side,
# deck (ao evalrig) on the left, stage (a shell the deck drives) on the right.
#
#   ./demo.sh

# Works inside or outside Zellij:
#   - inside Zellij  -> opens the demo as a new TAB (Zellij won't nest sessions).
#   - outside Zellij -> starts a new session.

#

# screen-record this two-pane session.
set -euo pipefail

here="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
repo="$(cd "$here/../.." && pwd)"
backend="$repo/backend"

for bin in zellij go; do

done

        }

    }
}"

1	// Package evalrig is the interactive control deck of the AO Adapter Proving
2	// Ground: a Bubble Tea TUI that renders the adapters × six-dimensions eval
3	// matrix and lets a presenter run cells one keypress at a time, driving a
4	// sibling Zellij "stage" pane to show each check executing live. The verdicts
5	// come from the same in-process conformance engine CI runs, so the demo and the
6	// regression guard can never disagree.
7	package evalrig
8	
9	import (
10		"context"
11		"fmt"
12		"strings"
13	
14		tea "github.com/charmbracelet/bubbletea"
15	
16		"github.com/aoagents/agent-orchestrator/backend/internal/evalrig/conformance"
17		"github.com/aoagents/agent-orchestrator/backend/internal/evalrig/registry"
18	)
19	
20	type cellState int
21	
22	const (
23		cellPending cellState = iota
24		cellRunning
25		cellDone
26	)
27	
28	// Model is the control-deck state.
29	type Model struct {
30		harnessed   []registry.HarnessAgent
31		dims        []string
32		state       map[string]map[string]cellState
33		result      map[string]map[string]conformance.Result
34		row, col    int
35		logs        []string
36		stage       *Stage
37		live        LiveConfig
38		liveSession *liveSession
39		liveCap     map[string]bool
40		width       int
41		quitting    bool
42	}
43	
44	// cellResultMsg carries a finished cell verdict back into Update.
45	type cellResultMsg struct {
46		harness string
47		dim     string
48		result  conformance.Result
49	}
50	
51	// New builds the deck over the registered adapters, a (possibly no-op) stage,
52	// and a (possibly disabled) live config.
53	func New(stage *Stage, live LiveConfig) Model {
54		harnessed := registry.Harnessed()
55		state := make(map[string]map[string]cellState, len(harnessed))
56		result := make(map[string]map[string]conformance.Result, len(harnessed))
57		for _, ha := range harnessed {
58			h := string(ha.Harness)
59			state[h] = map[string]cellState{}
60			result[h] = map[string]conformance.Result{}
61			for _, d := range conformance.Dimensions {
62				state[h][d] = cellPending
63			}
64		}
65		return Model{
66			harnessed: harnessed,
67			dims:      conformance.Dimensions,
68			state:     state,
69			result:    result,
70			stage:     stage,
71			live:      live,
72			liveCap:   map[string]bool{},
73		}
74	}
75	
76	// Init implements tea.Model.
77	func (m Model) Init() tea.Cmd { return nil }
78	
79	// Update implements tea.Model.
80	func (m Model) Update(msg tea.Msg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
81		switch msg := msg.(type) {
82		case tea.WindowSizeMsg:
83			m.width = msg.Width
84			return m, nil
85	
86		case cellResultMsg:
87			m.state[msg.harness][msg.dim] = cellDone
88			m.result[msg.harness][msg.dim] = msg.result
89			m.appendLog(fmt.Sprintf("%s/%s → %s", msg.harness, msg.dim, strings.ToUpper(string(msg.result.Status))))
90			return m, nil
91	
92		case liveSpawnResultMsg:
93			cmd := m.applyLiveSpawn(msg)
94			return m, cmd
95	
96		case livePollResultMsg:
97			cmd := m.applyLivePoll(msg)
98			return m, cmd
99	
100		case livePollTickMsg:
101			if m.liveSession != nil && m.liveSession.id == msg.id && !m.liveSession.terminated {
102				cmd := m.pollCmd(msg.id)
103				return m, cmd
104			}
105			return m, nil
106	
107		case tea.KeyMsg:
108			return m.handleKey(msg)
109		}
110		return m, nil
111	}
112	
113	func (m Model) handleKey(msg tea.KeyMsg) (tea.Model, tea.Cmd) {
114		switch msg.String() {
115		case "q", "ctrl+c", "esc":
116			m.quitting = true
117			return m, tea.Quit
118		case "up", "k":
119			m.row = clamp(m.row-1, len(m.harnessed)-1)
120		case "down", "j":
121			m.row = clamp(m.row+1, len(m.harnessed)-1)
122		case "left", "h":
123			m.col = clamp(m.col-1, len(m.dims)-1)
124		case "right", "l":
125			m.col = clamp(m.col+1, len(m.dims)-1)
126		case "enter":
127			// Run the selected cell, then advance to the next — the "keep pressing
128			// enter to run the next test" presenter flow.
129			cmd := m.runSelected()
130			m.advance()
131			return m, cmd
132		case " ", "r":
133			// Re-run the selected cell in place (no cursor advance).
134			cmd := m.runSelected()
135			return m, cmd
136		case "a":
137			// Run every dimension for the current adapter.
138			cmd := m.runRow(m.row)
139			return m, cmd
140		case "A":
141			// Run the whole matrix.
142			cmd := m.runAll()
143			return m, cmd
144		case "L":
145			// Live-spawn the selected adapter (if a daemon + project are configured).
146			cmd := m.startLive()
147			return m, cmd
148		case "x":
149			// Stop watching the current live session.
150			if m.liveSession != nil {
151				m.appendLog(fmt.Sprintf("live: stopped watching %s", m.liveSession.id))
152				m.liveSession = nil
153			}
154		}
155		return m, nil
156	}
157	
158	func (m *Model) runSelected() tea.Cmd {
159		// A deliberate single-cell run drives the stage so the audience watches the
160		// real test execute.
161		return m.runCell(m.row, m.col, true)
162	}
163	
164	// runCell runs one (adapter, dimension) check in-process. When showStage is
165	// true it also types the matching `go test` into the stage pane. Bulk runs pass
166	// false: typing dozens of commands into one shell would both flood it and — even
167	// serialized — queue behind each other, so they only update the matrix.
168	func (m *Model) runCell(row, col int, showStage bool) tea.Cmd {
169		ha := m.harnessed[row]
170		h := string(ha.Harness)
171		dim := m.dims[col]
172		if m.state[h][dim] == cellRunning {
173			return nil
174		}
175		m.state[h][dim] = cellRunning
176		m.appendLog(fmt.Sprintf("running %s/%s …", h, dim))
177		stage := m.stage
178		return func() tea.Msg {
179			ctx := context.Background()
180			if showStage {
181				_ = stage.Run(ctx, goTestCommand(h, dim))
182			}
183			res, _ := conformance.RunDimension(ctx, ha, dim)
184			return cellResultMsg{harness: h, dim: dim, result: res}
185		}
186	}
187	
188	func (m *Model) runRow(row int) tea.Cmd {
189		cmds := make([]tea.Cmd, 0, len(m.dims))
190		for c := range m.dims {
191			if cmd := m.runCell(row, c, false); cmd != nil {
192				cmds = append(cmds, cmd)
193			}
194		}
195		return tea.Batch(cmds...)
196	}
197	
198	func (m *Model) runAll() tea.Cmd {
199		cmds := make([]tea.Cmd, 0, len(m.harnessed)*len(m.dims))
200		for r := range m.harnessed {
201			for c := range m.dims {
202				if cmd := m.runCell(r, c, false); cmd != nil {
203					cmds = append(cmds, cmd)
204				}
205			}
206		}
207		return tea.Batch(cmds...)
208	}
209	
210	// advance moves the cursor to the next cell, left-to-right then down a row.
211	func (m *Model) advance() {
212		m.col++
213		if m.col >= len(m.dims) {
214			m.col = 0
215			if m.row < len(m.harnessed)-1 {
216				m.row++
217			} else {
218				m.col = len(m.dims) - 1 // stay on the last cell
219			}
220		}
221	}
222	
223	func (m *Model) appendLog(line string) {
224		m.logs = append(m.logs, line)
225		if len(m.logs) > 6 {
226			m.logs = m.logs[len(m.logs)-6:]
227		}
228	}
229	
230	// goTestCommand is the command the stage runs to demonstrate one cell: the real
231	// conformance subtest, in verbose mode, so the audience sees genuine PASS lines.
232	func goTestCommand(harness, dim string) string {
233		return fmt.Sprintf(
234			"go test ./internal/evalrig/conformance/ -run 'TestConformance/%s/%s' -v -count=1",
235			harness, dim,
236		)
237	}
238	
239	// clamp bounds v to [0, hi]; the cursor never goes below the first row/column.
240	func clamp(v, hi int) int {
241		if v < 0 {
242			return 0
243		}
244		if v > hi {
245			return hi
246		}
247		return v
248	}

# 🎯 Week Goal — Agent Orchestrator

**Owner:** Tanishq · **Set:** Tue Jun 2, 2026 · **Deadline:** Fri Jun 5, 2026 (EOD) — weekend = buffer
**Cadence:** Daily standup report to lead. One primary focus per day. Check a box, you made progress.

> **North star:** A daemon that spawns *real* agent sessions (not stubs) across multiple CLI agents with
> activity-detection hooks, plus a written, agreed plan for the in-app browser + annotation.

---

## ⚖️ Scope reality check (read this once, then stop worrying about it)

You have 6 tasks and ~4 working days. Not all 6 are "ship a finished feature" tasks — and that's fine:

| # | Task | Honest deliverable this week |
|---|------|------------------------------|
| 1 | Wire session manager → adapters | ✅ **Finishable** — ~80% done already |
| 2 | opencode adapter + hooks | ✅ **Finishable** — follows codex pattern |

| 6 | Browser annotation (agentation pkg) | 📐 **Design doc + spike** (depends on #4) |

---

### Task 4 — In-app browser, end-to-end  ·  `GREENFIELD (design)`  📐

Frontend is a bare Electron stub (`frontend/src/main.ts` loads `about:blank`). Deliverable = the plan.

- [ ] Write `docs/design/in-app-browser.md` — chosen approach, interfaces sketched, open questions, follow-up plan
- [ ] **Done when:** design doc exists + (stretch) a thrown-away spike proving the agent↔browser path

Depends on Task 4. Likely built on the `agentation` package.

- [ ] Research what `agentation` provides + how it'd plug into the Task 4 browser
- [ ] Write `docs/design/browser-annotation.md` — integration points, data model, open questions
- [ ] **Done when:** design doc exists with a chosen approach + follow-up implementation plan

> objectively checkable from that output.

1. **Force the proof into the transcript** — say "show the full output"; the check rides on commands Claude actually runs.
2. **Objective end-states only** — "file has sections X/Y/Z", "command exits 0". Never "clean"/"good" (the evaluator can't judge taste → never converges).

## 🚀 Run it: paste these into `/goal`

> `/goal` (Claude Code v2.1.139+, trusted workspace, hooks enabled) runs Claude autonomously turn after
> turn until a condition is met. A small evaluator model checks the condition **against what Claude
> surfaces in the transcript** — it does NOT run commands itself. Every condition below is written to be
> objectively checkable from that output.

**5 rules that make completion evaluate correctly:**

1. **Force the proof into the transcript** — say "show the full output"; the check rides on commands Claude actually runs.
2. **Objective end-states only** — "file has sections X/Y/Z", "command exits 0". Never "clean"/"good" (the evaluator can't judge taste → never converges).
3. **Anti-cheat guard** — "do not skip/delete/weaken any test", so the loop can't satisfy the evaluator by gutting the check.
4. **Bound open-ended work** — "exactly 2 adapters", not "all agents", or the loop never ends.
5. **One goal per task/day** — a week-long mega-goal isn't a single yes/no; it just burns tokens.
6. **Scope the test to what you changed** — `go test ./internal/daemon/...`, not `./...`. (Learned on Task 1: a pre-existing failure in unrelated in-progress code made `./...` red and would have sent the goal loop chasing a bug that wasn't ours.)

content.content:
# WebContentsView Summary

**What it is:** A View component that displays web content within an Electron application, inheriting from the `View` class.

**Deprecation note:** The documentation lists `BrowserView` as deprecated, suggesting `WebContentsView` is its modern replacement.

**Attachment & positioning:** Views are added to a window's content hierarchy using `win.contentView.addChildView(view)`, then positioned with the `setBounds()` method specifying coordinates and dimensions.

**Accessing webContents:** The `view.webContents` property provides access to the underlying WebContents object, enabling operations like `view.webContents.loadURL('https://example.com')`.

**Version info:** The documentation doesn't explicitly state the introduction version, though it's presented as current API in the latest docs.

content.content:
# Electron's Official Position on `<webview>`

**Not Recommended.** Electron explicitly warns against using the tag:

> "Electron's `webview` tag is based on Chromium's `webview`, which is undergoing dramatic architectural changes. This impacts the stability of `webviews`, including rendering, navigation, and event routing. We currently recommend to not use the `webview` tag and to consider alternatives."

**Recommended Alternatives:**
- `iframe`
- `WebContentsView`
- Architecture avoiding embedded content entirely

**Key Issues:**
- Runs in a separate process (unlike `iframe`)
- Architectural instability due to ongoing Chromium changes
- Known problems with rendering, navigation, and event routing
- Most methods require synchronous main process calls

The documentation makes clear this is a deprecated approach with significant stability concerns.

content.text:
Confirmed against Electron's own docs. Here's the renderer-option analysis, grounded in your Electron 33 setup and the thin-supervisor architecture.

## TL;DR — use `WebContentsView`

For Electron 33, this isn't close. `BrowserView` is deprecated, `<webview>` is *officially discouraged*, `iframe` can't be a real browser — `WebContentsView` is the one supported, stable option, and it happens to align perfectly with your "main process owns everything network" rule.

## The four candidates

| Option | Status (Electron 33) | Layout model | Where the page's `webContents` lives | Fit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`WebContentsView`** | ✅ Official, GA since v30 | Native overlay (composited at pixel bounds; not in the DOM) | **Main process** (`view.webContents`) | ✅ **Pick** |
| `<webview>` tag | ⚠️ "We recommend not to use it" — Chromium churn breaks rendering/nav/event routing; separate process; most methods need sync main calls | DOM element (flows in React layout) | Renderer (reach main via `getWebContentsId()`) | ✗ unstable |
| `BrowserView` | ⛔ Deprecated, slated for removal | Native overlay (same as WebContentsView) | Main process | ✗ deprecated |
| `iframe` | ✅ Stable | DOM element | Renderer (sandboxed) | ✗ not a browser |

`iframe` is a non-starter for a *browser*: most real sites send `X-Frame-Options`/`CSP frame-ancestors` that refuse to be framed, and you get no real navigation/driving control. Electron lists it as an "alternative," but only for cooperative embeds.

## Why `WebContentsView` is the right fit *for this app specifically*

1. **The browsed page's `webContents` lives in the main process** — which is exactly where your architecture already puts everything privileged. `main.ts` is the *only* layer that talks to the daemon ("daemon logic must not move into the UI surface"). Agent-driving the browser — `view.webContents.loadURL()`, `.executeJavaScript()`, CDP via `.debugger`, `.capturePage()` — all happens in main, reachable from the agent path **without the renderer in the loop**. So the renderer choice *pre-answers* design-doc question #3 (how agents drive/observe the browser): it's the same decision.
2. **Crash + security isolation** — the page is its own `WebContents`, sandboxed; it can't touch the React UI or your `preload` bridge.
3. **It's the only non-deprecated, non-discouraged option** — for a feature an agent must *reliably* drive, `<webview>`'s instability is disqualifying, and it wouldn't even save the main-process plumbing (you'd still bounce through `getWebContentsId()`).

## The one real cost — and how we pay it

`WebContentsView` is a **native overlay**, not a DOM node: it composites on top of the renderer at pixel coordinates, so it doesn't flow in React's layout. Three consequences, all standard patterns:

- **Bounds-sync** — put a placeholder `<div className="browser-slot">` in `sv-canvas`; a `ResizeObserver` (+ window resize + the `ResizablePanel` drag) computes its rect → IPC → `view.setBounds({x,y,width,height})`. ~30 lines.
- **z-order** — the view sits *above* renderer content, so React modals/menus can't visually overlap it. Render browser chrome (URL bar, tabs) as React *around* the slot, and hide the view (empty bounds / `removeChildView`) when a modal opens over it.
- **Lifecycle** — show/hide as `SessionView` opens/closes; one view per session vs. a shared singleton (open question below).

## Concrete wiring for this codebase

```
main.ts        ipcMain.handle("browser:create" | "navigate" | "setBounds" | "exec" | "destroy")
               → creates WebContentsView, win.contentView.addChildView(view)
preload.ts     window.ao.browser = { create, navigate, setBounds, onState, … }   (mirrors window.ao.request)
renderer       <BrowserPane> in SessionView's sv-canvas: the slot div + ResizeObserver → setBounds;
               a React URL bar / tabs above it; subscribes to nav-state events for back/forward/loading
```

It slots into the existing `sv-canvas` exactly where `<Terminal>` lives today — likely as a **tab or split** alongside the terminal (Terminal | Browser), which fits the `ResizablePanelGroup` already there.

## Open questions this surfaces (they feed the rest of the doc)

- **One `WebContentsView` per session, or one shared singleton** repositioned per active session? (memory vs. state-preservation)
- **How does the *agent* reach main's `webContents`?** Through the daemon (`ao browser …` command → daemon → ? ) or a more direct bridge? This is design-doc Q2/Q3 and is the meatiest decision — the renderer choice makes it *possible* in main, but doesn't decide the transport.
- **CDP exposure** — do we attach `webContents.debugger` (Chrome DevTools Protocol) so the agent gets the full automation surface (DOM, input, screenshots), or a narrower custom verb set?

Want me to (a) **capture this into `docs/design/in-app-browser.md`** (scaffold the doc, renderer section filled), (b) **spike it** — wire a minimal `WebContentsView` into `SessionView` to prove the bounds-sync + a `loadURL`, or (c) keep going and **tackle the agent↔browser mechanism** next (the harder question) before writing anything down?

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the VS Code Simple Browser extension implementation regarding iframe and webview architecture:

## Simple Browser Extension Overview

The Simple Browser extension uses a webview to render webpages directly in VS Code. It provides a very basic browser preview using an iframe embedded in a webview.

## Architecture and Limitations

The browser has a number of limitations due to the security around iframes, including that it traps keyboard focus, can't detect if a page fails to load, and can't track the current url of the iframe.

## Webview Architecture Details

A webview is like an iframe within VS Code that your extension controls. A webview can render almost any HTML content in this frame, and it communicates with extensions using message passing.

## Implementation Pattern

Webviews are implemented as isolated environments that communicate with the workbench via an asynchronous messaging bridge. To ensure security and performance, webviews are hosted in iframe elements (even in Electron) and utilize Service Workers for local resource loading.

The Simple Browser extension represents a practical implementation of VS Code's webview API, using nested iframes to display external web content while maintaining the security isolation that VS Code requires for webview environments.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about selecting DOM elements in preview, sending to AI coding agents, and how it integrates with dev servers:

## Key Tools and Approaches

### Stagewise
Stagewise started as a browser toolbar and is pivoting to a full "developer browser" (Electron-based). It runs `npx stagewise@latest` which starts a CLI proxy on port 3100 and injects a toolbar into your running app. It operates directly in your browser through a visual toolbar interface, allowing developers to select DOM elements and make AI-powered changes to their local codebase.

### Onlook
Onlook uses a sandboxed web container, not your real dev server. This makes it safer for experimentation but means it doesn't see your actual runtime environment — middleware, environment variables, real API responses, etc. However, you can always right-click an element to open up the exact location of the element in code.

### Frontman (Dev Server Middleware Approach)
Frontman installs as middleware inside your framework's dev server (Next.js, Astro, or Vite). Because it runs inside the framework, it has native access to both client-side context (DOM, component tree, computed styles, click targets) and server-side context (routes, compiled module graph, server logs, framework-specific state).

### Domscribe
For precise source mapping, Domscribe bridges both directions: click a DOM element to tell your agent what to change, or let your agent query any source location to see exactly what it looks like live in the browser. It walks your JSX and Vue templates, assigns each element a stable ID, and writes a manifest that maps every ID to its exact file, line, and column.

lastPrompt: I would also like to know how did vscode has implemented its in-app web browser.   My main concern is that would my users be able to annotate the UI elements/components of the rendered preview URL tha…

content.text:
Excellent question — and it's the one that actually *locks in* the renderer choice, because annotation = reaching into the page's DOM, and that's precisely where the iframe model dies and `WebContentsView` shines.

## How VS Code does it (and why you shouldn't copy it)

VS Code's **Simple Browser is an `<iframe>` inside a webview** — and VS Code webviews are *themselves* iframes (nested iframes for isolation), even on the desktop. ([webview API](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/extension-guides/webview), [simple-browser PR](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/109276), [Matt Bierner on webviews-on-web](https://blog.mattbierner.com/vscode-webview-web-learnings/)). The Simple Browser README itself lists the tells of the iframe wall: it "traps keyboard focus, can't detect if a page fails to load, and **can't track the current url of the iframe.**"

Why iframes, not Electron's native views? Because **VS Code must also run on the web** (vscode.dev / github.dev), where `BrowserView`/`WebContentsView` don't exist. So it standardized on iframe webviews for portability — and *ate* the limitations. **You're a desktop Electron app. You don't have that constraint, so you shouldn't inherit that ceiling.**

## The crux: the same-origin wall vs. privileged injection

This is the key technical point for your concern:

- An **`<iframe>`** loading a cross-origin URL is sealed by the **same-origin policy** — the parent page (your React UI) **cannot read or touch the iframe's DOM**. That's a browser security boundary, not a config you can flip. VS Code can't annotate arbitrary pages for exactly this reason.
- A **`WebContentsView`** is *not* a sibling frame — it's the embedder. Same-origin policy **does not apply** to how you reach into it. You get **two** privileged paths to the DOM **of any loaded URL**:
  1. **`webContents.executeJavaScript(...)`** — runs code *as the page* (like a DevTools console / content script). Full DOM read/write, draw overlays, capture selectors — on any origin.
  2. **`webContents.debugger`** = the **Chrome DevTools Protocol**. `DOM.getDocument` (the whole tree), `Overlay.highlightNode` (the literal inspector highlight), `DOM.getBoxModel`, `Runtime.evaluate`, input synthesis, screenshots — the same surface Playwright/Puppeteer/Chrome DevTools use.

Both run **from the main process** — which, again, is exactly where your architecture already wants privileged work.

## So: yes, your users can annotate UI elements/components — here's the honest breakdown

| What you want to annotate | Mechanism | What you get |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw DOM elements** of *any* preview URL | `executeJavaScript` or CDP `DOM`/`Overlay` | element under cursor, bounding box, CSS selector, highlight overlay |
| **Components** (e.g. "the `<Sidebar>`") of *the user's own app* | injection **+ a build-time source map** | DOM node → React component → **`file:line:col`**, so the agent edits the right source |

The second row is the rich one you're really asking about. Raw DOM you get for free; **component-level** annotation needs the page to *carry* source info — which you add with a **Vite plugin** (you already use Vite) that stamps `data-ao-source="file:line"` on each element at build time, or by reading React fiber's `_debugSource` in dev. Then "user circled this button" becomes "edit `Sidebar.tsx:42`."

This is well-trodden — every serious "see your frontend" tool works this way, none of them via a plain iframe ([overview](https://dev.to/bluehotdog/ai-coding-tools-that-actually-see-your-browser-2026-2hoc)):
- **[stagewise](https://github.com/stagewise-io/stagewise)** — injects a toolbar into your running app (CLI proxy on :3100), select element → AI edits source; now pivoting to an **Electron "developer browser"** (same conclusion you're reaching).
- **[Onlook](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook)** — Electron, right-click element → jump to exact source location.
- **[Frontman](https://frontman.sh/)** — dev-server middleware → native DOM + component tree + computed styles.
- **[Domscribe](https://www.domscribe.com/)** — walks JSX/Vue, assigns each element a stable ID, writes a manifest mapping ID → file:line:col (bidirectional).
- **[Chrome DevTools MCP](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp)** — the CDP-for-agents path.

## What this means for the design

**The annotation requirement is the strongest argument for `WebContentsView` and against the VS Code iframe model.** It doesn't just *allow* DOM annotation — it's the only one of the four options that does, on arbitrary URLs.

Concrete shape for component annotation:
```
Vite plugin (user's app)   stamps data-ao-source="src/.../Sidebar.tsx:42:7" on elements
main.ts                    after loadURL → executeJavaScript(annotationOverlay.js) into the view
overlay (in-page)          hover/click → reads data-ao-source + selector + box → postMessage
preload/main               receives annotation → window.ao + daemon → agent context (this is Task 6 / "agentation")
CDP (fallback)             for non-instrumented URLs: DOM/Overlay/box-model gives selector+highlight, no source
```

One real **open question for Task 6**: draw the highlight **in-page** (injected overlay div — pixel-perfect, follows scroll, but lives in the page) vs. **above** (a transparent overlay synced via CDP box-models — cleaner separation, more coordinate plumbing). Most tools do in-page.

Want me to (a) **fold this into the design doc** as the "renderer + DOM-access" section (this is genuinely the heart of it), (b) **spike the proof** — `WebContentsView` + `loadURL` + `executeJavaScript` that returns the DOM element under a click, to *prove* the annotation path end-to-end, or (c) dig into the **agent↔browser transport** (how the annotation/drive actually reaches the agent — daemon command vs. MCP tool vs. IPC)?

# In-App Browser — Design

**Status:** Draft · renderer + DOM-access **decided**; backend surface and agent transport **open**.
**Task:** Week goal Task 4 (greenfield). Foundation for Task 6 (browser annotation).

## Goal

A pane in the desktop app that renders a live **preview URL** of the app the user is
building, that the user **and** AO agents can both **drive** (navigate, reload, interact)
and — critically — **annotate**: point at a UI element/component in the preview and attach
it as context for an agent ("change *this* button"). Annotation requires reaching into the
previewed page's **rendered DOM**, which is the constraint that drives the renderer choice.

Non-goals (this doc): the full annotation UX/data model (Task 6), and a general-purpose web
browser. The target is *previews of the user's own running app*, with arbitrary URLs as a
secondary case.

## Decision 1 — Renderer: `WebContentsView`

Electron `^33.0.0` (see `frontend/package.json`) settles the field:

| Option | Status (Electron 33) | Layout model | Page's `webContents` | DOM access for annotation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`WebContentsView`** | ✅ Official, GA since v30 | Native overlay (pixel bounds; not in the DOM) | **Main process** | ✅ full, any URL (see Decision 2) |
| `<webview>` tag | ⚠️ Officially discouraged — Chromium churn breaks rendering/nav/event routing; sync main calls | DOM element (flows in React) | Renderer (reach main via `getWebContentsId()`) | ⚠️ possible but unstable host |
| `BrowserView` | ⛔ Deprecated, slated for removal | Native overlay | Main process | (superseded by `WebContentsView`) |
| `iframe` | ✅ Stable | DOM element | Renderer (sandboxed) | ⛔ blocked cross-origin (same-origin policy) |

**Chosen: `WebContentsView`.** Reasons, in priority order:

1. **DOM access for annotation works on any URL** (Decision 2) — the deciding factor. The
   iframe approach cannot do this; `<webview>` can but on an unstable foundation.
2. **The page's `webContents` lives in the main process**, which is exactly where this app's
   architecture already puts privileged work: `frontend/src/main.ts` is the *only* layer that
   talks to the daemon ("daemon logic must not move into the UI surface"). Agent-driving —
   `loadURL`, `executeJavaScript`, CDP via `webContents.debugger`, `capturePage` — happens in
   main, reachable from the agent path **without the renderer in the loop**.
3. **Crash + security isolation** — the previewed page is its own sandboxed `WebContents`; it
   cannot touch the React UI or the `preload` bridge.
4. **Only non-deprecated, non-discouraged option** for Electron 33.

**The cost, and how we pay it.** `WebContentsView` is a *native overlay*: it composites on top
of the renderer at pixel coordinates and does **not** flow in React's layout. Three standard
consequences:

- **Bounds-sync** — a placeholder `<div className="browser-slot">` in `SessionView`'s
  `sv-canvas`; a `ResizeObserver` (+ window resize + the `ResizablePanel` drag) computes its
  rect → IPC → `view.setBounds({x,y,width,height})`. ~30 lines.
- **z-order** — the view sits *above* renderer content, so React modals/menus can't overlap
  it. Render browser chrome (URL bar, tabs) as React *around* the slot; hide the view (empty
  bounds / `removeChildView`) when a modal opens over it.
- **Lifecycle** — show/hide as `SessionView` opens/closes (see open question on per-session
  vs singleton).

It slots into `SessionView`'s `sv-canvas` exactly where `<Terminal>` lives today — likely a
tab or split alongside it (Terminal | Browser), fitting the existing `ResizablePanelGroup`.

## Decision 2 — DOM access for annotation (the deciding factor)

Annotation = reaching into the previewed page's DOM. The dividing line is the **same-origin
policy**:

- An **`<iframe>`** loading a cross-origin URL is sealed: the parent (our React UI) cannot
  read or touch its DOM. This is a browser security boundary, not a flag. (This is why VS
  Code's Simple Browser "can't track the current url of the iframe" — see below.)
- A **`WebContentsView`** is the *embedder*, not a sibling frame, so same-origin policy does
  not gate how we reach in. Two privileged paths to the DOM of **any** loaded URL, both from
  main:
  1. **`webContents.executeJavaScript(code)`** — runs *as the page* (like a DevTools console
     / content script): read/write DOM, draw overlays, capture selectors. Any origin.
  2. **`webContents.debugger`** = the **Chrome DevTools Protocol**: `DOM.getDocument` (full
     tree), `Overlay.highlightNode` (the inspector highlight), `DOM.getBoxModel`,
     `Runtime.evaluate`, input synthesis, screenshots. The Playwright/DevTools surface.

What each gets us:

| Target | Mechanism | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw DOM element** of *any* preview URL | `executeJavaScript` or CDP `DOM`/`Overlay` | element under cursor, box, selector, highlight |
| **Component** (e.g. `<Sidebar>`) of *the user's own app* | injection **+ build-time source map** | DOM node → React component → **`file:line:col`** so the agent edits the right source |

Raw DOM is free. **Component-level** annotation needs the page to *carry* source info — added
with a **Vite plugin** (this app already uses Vite) that stamps `data-ao-source="file:line"`
on elements at build time, or by reading React fiber `_debugSource` in dev. Then "user circled
this button" becomes "edit `Sidebar.tsx:42`."

This is the established pattern — every "see your frontend" tool works this way, none via a
plain iframe: **stagewise** (injects a toolbar into the running app; now pivoting to an
Electron browser — same conclusion), **Onlook** (Electron; right-click element → source),
**Frontman** (dev-server middleware → DOM + component tree), **Domscribe** (stamps stable IDs
→ file:line:col manifest), **Chrome DevTools MCP** (the CDP-for-agents path).

## How VS Code does it (and why we diverge)

VS Code's **Simple Browser is an `<iframe>` inside a webview**, and VS Code webviews are
themselves iframes (nested for isolation), even on desktop. It does this because **VS Code must
also run on the web** (vscode.dev), where Electron's native views don't exist — so it
standardized on iframes for portability and accepted the limits (its own README: the browser
"traps keyboard focus, can't detect if a page fails to load, and can't track the current url of
the iframe").

**We are desktop-only Electron and have no web-portability constraint, so we do not inherit that
ceiling.** Copying the iframe model would forfeit cross-origin DOM access — i.e. the annotation
feature — which is the whole point.

## Concrete wiring (renderer + annotation)

```
Vite plugin (user's app)   stamps data-ao-source="src/.../Sidebar.tsx:42:7" on elements
main.ts                    ipcMain.handle("browser:create"|"navigate"|"setBounds"|"exec"|"destroy")
                           → new WebContentsView; win.contentView.addChildView(view)
                           → after loadURL: webContents.executeJavaScript(annotationOverlay.js)
preload.ts                 window.ao.browser = { create, navigate, setBounds, onState, onAnnotate }
                           (mirrors the existing window.ao.request bridge)
renderer (<BrowserPane>)   slot div + ResizeObserver → setBounds; React URL bar / tabs around it;
                           subscribes to nav-state + annotation events
overlay (in-page script)   hover/click → reads data-ao-source + selector + box model → postMessage
                           → main → window.ao + daemon → agent context  (this is Task 6 / "agentation")
CDP (fallback)             for non-instrumented URLs: DOM/Overlay/box-model → selector + highlight,
                           no source mapping
```

## Open questions (still to decide)

These feed the rest of Task 4 and into Task 6.

- **(b) Backend surface** — what does the daemon expose for the browser? Candidates: a session
  carries a "preview URL"; daemon endpoints to set/get it and to relay drive/annotate commands;
  or the browser stays a pure FE+main concern and the daemon only stores the preview URL on the
  session. *Undecided.*
- **(c) Agent ↔ browser transport** — how does an agent actually drive/observe the browser?
  Candidates: (i) an `ao browser <verb>` CLI surface → daemon → FE; (ii) an **MCP tool** the
  agent calls; (iii) direct IPC. The renderer choice makes driving *possible in main*; it does
  not pick the transport. **This is the meatiest remaining decision.**
- **One `WebContentsView` per session vs. a shared singleton** repositioned per active session
  (memory vs. state preservation).
- **Overlay rendering** — in-page injected overlay (pixel-perfect, follows scroll, lives in the
  page) vs. a transparent overlay synced via CDP box-models (cleaner separation, more coordinate
  plumbing). Most tools do in-page.
- **CDP exposure scope** — attach `webContents.debugger` for the full automation surface, or a
  narrower custom verb set?

## Follow-up plan

1. Decide **(c) agent↔browser transport** and **(b) backend surface** (next working session).
2. Throwaway **spike**: `WebContentsView` in `SessionView` + `loadURL` + `executeJavaScript`
   returning the DOM element (and `data-ao-source`) under a click — proves the annotation path
   end-to-end.
3. Write the **Vite source-stamp plugin** (small) so component-level mapping is real.
4. Hand the annotation overlay + capture model to **Task 6 / `docs/design/browser-annotation.md`**.

## References

- Electron — [`WebContentsView`](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/web-contents-view),
  [`<webview>` tag (discouraged)](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/webview-tag)
- VS Code — [Webview API](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/extension-guides/webview),
  [simple-browser PR #109276](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/109276),
  [webviews on the web (Bierner)](https://blog.mattbierner.com/vscode-webview-web-learnings/)
- Prior art — [stagewise](https://github.com/stagewise-io/stagewise),
  [Onlook](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook), [Frontman](https://frontman.sh/),
  [Domscribe](https://www.domscribe.com/),

# In-App Browser — Design

**Status:** Draft · renderer + DOM-access **decided**; backend surface and agent transport **open**.
**Task:** Week goal Task 4 (greenfield). Foundation for Task 6 (browser annotation).

## Goal

A pane in the desktop app that renders a live **preview URL** of the app the user is
building, that the user **and** AO agents can both **drive** (navigate, reload, interact)
and — critically — **annotate**: point at a UI element/component in the preview and attach
it as context for an agent ("change *this* button"). Annotation requires reaching into the
previewed page's **rendered DOM**, which is the constraint that drives the renderer choice.

Non-goals (this doc): the full annotation UX/data model (Task 6), and a general-purpose web
browser. The target is *previews of the user's own running app*, with arbitrary URLs as a
secondary case.

## Decision 1 — Renderer: `WebContentsView`

Electron `^33.0.0` (see `frontend/package.json`) settles the field:

| Option | Status (Electron 33) | Layout model | Page's `webContents` | DOM access for annotation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **`WebContentsView`** | ✅ Official, GA since v30 | Native overlay (pixel bounds; not in the DOM) | **Main process** | ✅ full, any URL (see Decision 2) |
| `<webview>` tag | ⚠️ Officially discouraged — Chromium churn breaks rendering/nav/event routing; sync main calls | DOM element (flows in React) | Renderer (reach main via `getWebContentsId()`) | ⚠️ possible but unstable host |
| `BrowserView` | ⛔ Deprecated, slated for removal | Native overlay | Main process | (superseded by `WebContentsView`) |
| `iframe` | ✅ Stable | DOM element | Renderer (sandboxed) | ⛔ blocked cross-origin (same-origin policy) |

**Chosen: `WebContentsView`.** Reasons, in priority order:

1. **DOM access for annotation works on any URL** (Decision 2) — the deciding factor. The
   iframe approach cannot do this; `<webview>` can but on an unstable foundation.
2. **The page's `webContents` lives in the main process**, which is exactly where this app's
   architecture already puts privileged work: `frontend/src/main.ts` is the *only* layer that
   talks to the daemon ("daemon logic must not move into the UI surface"). Agent-driving —
   `loadURL`, `executeJavaScript`, CDP via `webContents.debugger`, `capturePage` — happens in
   main, reachable from the agent path **without the renderer in the loop**.
3. **Crash + security isolation** — the previewed page is its own sandboxed `WebContents`; it
   cannot touch the React UI or the `preload` bridge.
4. **Only non-deprecated, non-discouraged option** for Electron 33.

**The cost, and how we pay it.** `WebContentsView` is a *native overlay*: it composites on top
of the renderer at pixel coordinates and does **not** flow in React's layout. Three standard
consequences:

- **Bounds-sync** — a placeholder `<div className="browser-slot">` in `SessionView`'s
  `sv-canvas`; a `ResizeObserver` (+ window resize + the `ResizablePanel` drag) computes its
  rect → IPC → `view.setBounds({x,y,width,height})`. ~30 lines.
- **z-order** — the view sits *above* renderer content, so React modals/menus can't overlap
  it. Render browser chrome (URL bar, tabs) as React *around* the slot; hide the view (empty
  bounds / `removeChildView`) when a modal opens over it.
- **Lifecycle** — show/hide as `SessionView` opens/closes (see open question on per-session
  vs singleton).

It slots into `SessionView`'s `sv-canvas` exactly where `<Terminal>` lives today — likely a
tab or split alongside it (Terminal | Browser), fitting the existing `ResizablePanelGroup`.

## Decision 2 — DOM access for annotation (the deciding factor)

Annotation = reaching into the previewed page's DOM. The dividing line is the **same-origin
policy**:

- An **`<iframe>`** loading a cross-origin URL is sealed: the parent (our React UI) cannot
  read or touch its DOM. This is a browser security boundary, not a flag. (This is why VS
  Code's Simple Browser "can't track the current url of the iframe" — see below.)
- A **`WebContentsView`** is the *embedder*, not a sibling frame, so same-origin policy does
  not gate how we reach in. Two privileged paths to the DOM of **any** loaded URL, both from
  main:
  1. **`webContents.executeJavaScript(code)`** — runs *as the page* (like a DevTools console
     / content script): read/write DOM, draw overlays, capture selectors. Any origin.
  2. **`webContents.debugger`** = the **Chrome DevTools Protocol**: `DOM.getDocument` (full
     tree), `Overlay.highlightNode` (the inspector highlight), `DOM.getBoxModel`,
     `Runtime.evaluate`, input synthesis, screenshots. The Playwright/DevTools surface.

What each gets us:

| Target | Mechanism | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **Raw DOM element** of *any* preview URL | `executeJavaScript` or CDP `DOM`/`Overlay` | element under cursor, box, selector, highlight |
| **Component** (e.g. `<Sidebar>`) of *the user's own app* | injection **+ build-time source map** | DOM node → React component → **`file:line:col`** so the agent edits the right source |

Raw DOM is free. **Component-level** annotation needs the page to *carry* source info — added
with a **Vite plugin** (this app already uses Vite) that stamps `data-ao-source="file:line"`
on elements at build time, or by reading React fiber `_debugSource` in dev. Then "user circled
this button" becomes "edit `Sidebar.tsx:42`."

This is the established pattern — every "see your frontend" tool works this way, none via a
plain iframe: **stagewise** (injects a toolbar into the running app; now pivoting to an
Electron browser — same conclusion), **Onlook** (Electron; right-click element → source),
**Frontman** (dev-server middleware → DOM + component tree), **Domscribe** (stamps stable IDs
→ file:line:col manifest), **Chrome DevTools MCP** (the CDP-for-agents path).

## How VS Code does it (and why we diverge)

VS Code's **Simple Browser is an `<iframe>` inside a webview**, and VS Code webviews are
themselves iframes (nested for isolation), even on desktop. It does this because **VS Code must
also run on the web** (vscode.dev), where Electron's native views don't exist — so it
standardized on iframes for portability and accepted the limits (its own README: the browser
"traps keyboard focus, can't detect if a page fails to load, and can't track the current url of
the iframe").

**We are desktop-only Electron and have no web-portability constraint, so we do not inherit that
ceiling.** Copying the iframe model would forfeit cross-origin DOM access — i.e. the annotation
feature — which is the whole point.

## Concrete wiring (renderer + annotation)

```
Vite plugin (user's app)   stamps data-ao-source="src/.../Sidebar.tsx:42:7" on elements
main.ts                    ipcMain.handle("browser:create"|"navigate"|"setBounds"|"exec"|"destroy")
                           → new WebContentsView; win.contentView.addChildView(view)
                           → after loadURL: webContents.executeJavaScript(annotationOverlay.js)
preload.ts                 window.ao.browser = { create, navigate, setBounds, onState, onAnnotate }
                           (mirrors the existing window.ao.request bridge)
renderer (<BrowserPane>)   slot div + ResizeObserver → setBounds; React URL bar / tabs around it;
                           subscribes to nav-state + annotation events
overlay (in-page script)   hover/click → reads data-ao-source + selector + box model → postMessage
                           → main → window.ao + daemon → agent context  (this is Task 6 / "agentation")
CDP (fallback)             for non-instrumented URLs: DOM/Overlay/box-model → selector + highlight,
                           no source mapping
```

## Open questions (still to decide)

These feed the rest of Task 4 and into Task 6.

- **(b) Backend surface** — what does the daemon expose for the browser? Candidates: a session
  carries a "preview URL"; daemon endpoints to set/get it and to relay drive/annotate commands;
  or the browser stays a pure FE+main concern and the daemon only stores the preview URL on the
  session. *Undecided.*
- **(c) Agent ↔ browser transport** — how does an agent actually drive/observe the browser?
  Candidates: (i) an `ao browser <verb>` CLI surface → daemon → FE; (ii) an **MCP tool** the
  agent calls; (iii) direct IPC. The renderer choice makes driving *possible in main*; it does
  not pick the transport. **This is the meatiest remaining decision.**
- **One `WebContentsView` per session vs. a shared singleton** repositioned per active session
  (memory vs. state preservation).
- **Overlay rendering** — in-page injected overlay (pixel-perfect, follows scroll, lives in the
  page) vs. a transparent overlay synced via CDP box-models (cleaner separation, more coordinate
  plumbing). Most tools do in-page.
- **CDP exposure scope** — attach `webContents.debugger` for the full automation surface, or a
  narrower custom verb set?

## Follow-up plan

1. Decide **(c) agent↔browser transport** and **(b) backend surface** (next working session).
2. Throwaway **spike**: `WebContentsView` in `SessionView` + `loadURL` + `executeJavaScript`
   returning the DOM element (and `data-ao-source`) under a click — proves the annotation path
   end-to-end.
3. Write the **Vite source-stamp plugin** (small) so component-level mapping is real.
4. Hand the annotation overlay + capture model to **Task 6 / `docs/design/browser-annotation.md`**.

## References

- Electron — [`WebContentsView`](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/web-contents-view),
  [`<webview>` tag (discouraged)](https://www.electronjs.org/docs/latest/api/webview-tag)
- VS Code — [Webview API](https://code.visualstudio.com/api/extension-guides/webview),
  [simple-browser PR #109276](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/pull/109276),
  [webviews on the web (Bierner)](https://blog.mattbierner.com/vscode-webview-web-learnings/)
- Prior art — [stagewise](https://github.com/stagewise-io/stagewise),
  [Onlook](https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook), [Frontman](https://frontman.sh/),
  [Domscribe](https://www.domscribe.com/),
  [Chrome DevTools MCP](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-devtools-mcp),
  [overview](https://dev.to/bluehotdog/ai-coding-tools-that-actually-see-your-browser-2026-2hoc)

content.text:
Grounded. Two facts that decide this:

1. **The desktop app *polls* the daemon today** (`App.tsx`: `setInterval(poll, POLL_MS)`; `SessionView` every 2s) — there's **no** daemon→app push channel yet.
2. But the backend already has the **CDC broadcaster** built for exactly this: `cdc/poller.go` tails `change_log`, `cdc/broadcast.go` `Subscribe(fn)` fans out, and `cdc/event.go` literally says *"Future SSE/event endpoints can subscribe here too… subscribers track their own offset (SSE Last-Event-ID)."* The push rail is half-built; no HTTP endpoint exposes it yet.

## The decision: agent↔browser transport

**Core insight:** the agent (a CLI process in a worktree) and the browser (the `WebContentsView` in the Electron app) are in **different processes that share only the daemon**. So the daemon *must* broker — and it's the right hub anyway (it already owns sessions, the CLI surface, and the event bus).

```
agent (CLI, worktree) ──HTTP──► daemon ◄──HTTP/SSE──► Electron app (owns the WebContentsView)
        ao browser …         (session "browser"        executes on webContents
        annotations           capability + broker)      (executeJS / CDP), posts results back
```

**Recommendation — a daemon-brokered session "browser" capability:**
- **Agent surface:** `ao browser <verb>` CLI → `POST /sessions/{id}/browser/…`. Universal (every adapter can shell out; mirrors `ao hooks` / `ao send`). An **MCP tool** is a thin wrapper over the same daemon API — a fast-follow for the MCP-capable agents (claude-code/codex/cursor), not the foundation.
- **Executor:** the Electron app *registers* as the session's browser executor and runs commands on the `WebContentsView`. (Treating "executor" as a capability — not hardwired to Electron — leaves room for a headless one later.)
- **Push:** build the **SSE endpoint over the existing CDC broadcaster** — it's the intended direction and the only piece of genuinely new infra.

**The natural v1 / v2 split** (this is what makes it "quick"):
- **v1 — observe** (matches your annotation concern): user annotates an element → Electron **POSTs** annotation (selector + `data-ao-source` + screenshot) to the daemon → it lands as agent context. This is **Electron→daemon only — no push channel needed**, so it ships fast and delivers the actual goal (user annotates UI → agent acts).
- **v2 — drive** (agent → browser): needs the daemon→Electron **SSE** push. Build it second.

# Agentation: Visual Feedback Tool for AI Agents

## (1) Selection Mechanism
Agentation is a **React 18+ library** installed via npm. Users import and add the `<Agentation />` component to their app. The toolbar appears in the bottom-right corner, and users activate it to click elements for annotation. It supports click selection, text selection, multi-select via dragging, and area selection.

## (2) Element Reference Capture
The tool captures **CSS selectors and element positions**. According to the docs: "Agentation captures class names, selectors, and element positions so AI agents can `grep` for the exact code you're referring to."

## (3) Annotation Data Model
The repo doesn't expose the internal data structure in this content, but it produces **structured markdown output** that includes selectors, positions, and context about annotated elements.

## (4) Data Delivery to AI Agents
Users **copy structured output to clipboard**. The description states: "Copy markdown with selectors, positions, and context." This clipboard data can then be pasted into prompts for AI coding agents.

## (5) Tech Stack & Key Directories
- **Languages**: TypeScript (84.1%), SCSS (9.0%), HTML/CSS (3.3% each)
- **Key directories**: `/package` (npm package), `/mcp` (likely Model Context Protocol integration), `/skills`
- **Build files**: `package.json`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml`, `vercel.json` (deployment)
- **License**: PolyForm Shield 1.0.0

# Agentation MCP Overview

## Files in the Directory
The `mcp` directory contains:
- `src/` (source code folder)
- `.gitignore`
- `README.md`
- `package.json`
- `pnpm-lock.yaml`
- `tsconfig.json`
- `tsup.config.ts`

## Server Function
The MCP server provides visual feedback integration for AI coding agents by managing annotations created through a browser toolbar.

## MCP Tools Exposed
The server exposes eight tools:
- `agentation_list_sessions`
- `agentation_get_session`
- `agentation_get_pending`
- `agentation_get_all_pending`
- `agentation_acknowledge`
- `agentation_resolve`
- `agentation_dismiss`
- `agentation_reply`
- `agentation_watch_annotations`

## Annotation Reception Method
Annotations arrive via an **HTTP server** (default port 4747). The server accepts POST requests to create annotations and provides a Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream at `GET /sessions/:id/events` for real-time updates.

## Agent Connection
Agents connect through the MCP protocol using stdio. Installation is simplified with:
```
claude mcp add agentation -- npx agentation-mcp server
```
The server simultaneously runs the HTTP endpoint and exposes the MCP tools for Claude Code integration.

- `tsup.config.ts`

## Server Function
The MCP server provides visual feedback integration for AI coding agents by managing annotations created through a browser toolbar.

## MCP Tools Exposed
The server exposes eight tools:
- `agentation_list_sessions`
- `agentation_get_session`
- `agentation_get_pending`
- `agentation_get_all_pending`
- `agentation_acknowledge`
- `agentation_resolve`
- `agentation_dismiss`
- `agentation_reply`
- `agentation_watch_annotations`

## Annotation Reception Method
Annotations arrive via an **HTTP server** (default port 4747). The server accepts POST requests to create annotations and provides a Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream at `GET /sessions/:id/events` for real-time updates.

## Agent Connection
Agents connect through the MCP protocol using stdio. Installation is simplified with:
```
claude mcp add agentation -- npx agentation-mcp server
```
The server simultaneously runs the HTTP endpoint and exposes the MCP tools for Claude Code integration.

1. **Renderer** → `WebContentsView` (Electron 33; the only supported + DOM-accessible option)

```ts
// ── ao:mux — WebSocket terminal mux relay ───────────────────────────────────
//
// The renderer is sandboxed and cannot open sockets, so the single mux
// WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/mux lives here in main and frames are
// relayed to the renderer over IPC (mirrors the ao:request bridge above).
// Protocol: backend/internal/terminal/protocol.go.

import type { WebContents } from "electron";

interface MuxClientFrame {
  ch: "terminal" | "system";
  id?: string;
  type: "open" | "data" | "resize" | "close" | "ping";
  data?: string;
  cols?: number;
  rows?: number;
}

interface MuxServerFrame {
  ch?: string;
  id?: string;
  type?: string;
  data?: string;
  error?: string;
}

/** One renderer's view of the mux: its WebContents plus the panes it opened. */
interface MuxConn {
  ws: WebSocket | null;
  ready: boolean;
  // Frames queued while the socket is still CONNECTING.
  pending: MuxClientFrame[];
  // Pane handle ids this renderer has open (for replay/cleanup).
  open: Set<string>;
}

const muxConns = new Map<number, MuxConn>();

function muxURL(): string {
  // Reuse the existing port discovery; just swap http→ws.
  return `ws://127.0.0.1:${discoverPort()}/mux`;
}

function getMuxConn(wc: WebContents): MuxConn {
  let conn = muxConns.get(wc.id);
  if (conn) return conn;
  conn = { ws: null, ready: false, pending: [], open: new Set() };
  muxConns.set(wc.id, conn);

  const ws = new WebSocket(muxURL());
  conn.ws = ws;

  ws.on("open", () => {
    conn!.ready = true;
    for (const frame of conn!.pending) ws.send(JSON.stringify(frame));
    conn!.pending = [];
  });

  ws.on("message", (raw: WebSocket.RawData) => {
    if (wc.isDestroyed()) return;
    let frame: MuxServerFrame;
    try {
      frame = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) as MuxServerFrame;
    } catch {
      return;
    }
    // Liveness pong / session channel frames are ignored by the terminal UI.
    if (frame.ch !== "terminal" || !frame.id) return;
    wc.send(`ao:mux:msg:${frame.id}`, frame);
  });

  const teardown = (): void => {
    conn!.ready = false;
    conn!.ws = null;
    muxConns.delete(wc.id);
  };
  ws.on("close", teardown);
  ws.on("error", teardown);

  return conn;
}

function muxSend(wc: WebContents, frame: MuxClientFrame): void {
  const conn = getMuxConn(wc);
  if (conn.ready && conn.ws && conn.ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
    conn.ws.send(JSON.stringify(frame));
  } else {
    conn.pending.push(frame);
  }
}

function registerMuxIpc(): void {
  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:open", (event, handleId: string) => {
    const wc = event.sender;
    getMuxConn(wc).open.add(handleId);
    muxSend(wc, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "open" });
  });

  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:send", (event, handleId: string, data: string) => {
    muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "data", data });
  });

  ipcMain.handle(
    "ao:mux:resize",
    (event, handleId: string, cols: number, rows: number) => {
      muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "resize", cols, rows });
    },
  );

  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:close", (event, handleId: string) => {
    const conn = muxConns.get(event.sender.id);
    if (conn) conn.open.delete(handleId);
    muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "close" });
  });
}
```

  request: <T = unknown>(req: AoRequest): Promise<AoResponse<T>> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:request", req),

  mux: {
    open: (handleId: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:open", handleId),
    send: (handleId: string, data: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:send", handleId, data),
    resize: (handleId: string, cols: number, rows: number): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:resize", handleId, cols, rows),
    close: (handleId: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:close", handleId),

    // Returns an unsubscribe fn. Main pushes terminal frames on a
    // per-handle channel; we filter to {type:"data"} / {type:"exited"} here.
    onData: (handleId: string, cb: (b64: string) => void): (() => void) => {
      const channel = `ao:mux:msg:${handleId}`;
      const listener = (
        _e: Electron.IpcRendererEvent,
        frame: { type?: string; data?: string },
      ): void => {
        if (frame.type === "data" && typeof frame.data === "string") cb(frame.data);
      };
      ipcRenderer.on(channel, listener);
      return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, listener);
    },

    onExit: (handleId: string, cb: () => void): (() => void) => {
      const channel = `ao:mux:msg:${handleId}`;
      const listener = (
        _e: Electron.IpcRendererEvent,
        frame: { type?: string },
      ): void => {
        if (frame.type === "exited") cb();
      };
      ipcRenderer.on(channel, listener);
      return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, listener);
    },
  },
};

contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld("ao", api);

export type AoBridge = typeof api;

// ── ao:mux — WebSocket terminal mux relay ───────────────────────────────────
//
// The renderer is sandboxed and cannot open sockets, so the single mux
// WebSocket to ws://127.0.0.1:<port>/mux lives here in main and frames are
// relayed to the renderer over IPC (mirrors the ao:request bridge above).
// Protocol: backend/internal/terminal/protocol.go.

import type { WebContents } from "electron";

interface MuxClientFrame {
  ch: "terminal" | "system";
  id?: string;
  type: "open" | "data" | "resize" | "close" | "ping";
  data?: string;
  cols?: number;
  rows?: number;
}

interface MuxServerFrame {
  ch?: string;
  id?: string;
  type?: string;
  data?: string;
  error?: string;
}

/** One renderer's view of the mux: its WebContents plus the panes it opened. */
interface MuxConn {
  ws: WebSocket | null;
  ready: boolean;
  // Frames queued while the socket is still CONNECTING.
  pending: MuxClientFrame[];
  // Pane handle ids this renderer has open (for replay/cleanup).
  open: Set<string>;
}

const muxConns = new Map<number, MuxConn>();

function muxURL(): string {
  // Reuse the existing port discovery; just swap http→ws.
  return `ws://127.0.0.1:${discoverPort()}/mux`;
}

function getMuxConn(wc: WebContents): MuxConn {
  let conn = muxConns.get(wc.id);
  if (conn) return conn;
  conn = { ws: null, ready: false, pending: [], open: new Set() };
  muxConns.set(wc.id, conn);

  const ws = new WebSocket(muxURL());
  conn.ws = ws;

  ws.on("open", () => {
    conn!.ready = true;
    for (const frame of conn!.pending) ws.send(JSON.stringify(frame));
    conn!.pending = [];
  });

  ws.on("message", (raw: WebSocket.RawData) => {
    if (wc.isDestroyed()) return;
    let frame: MuxServerFrame;
    try {
      frame = JSON.parse(raw.toString()) as MuxServerFrame;
    } catch {
      return;
    }
    // Liveness pong / session channel frames are ignored by the terminal UI.
    if (frame.ch !== "terminal" || !frame.id) return;
    wc.send(`ao:mux:msg:${frame.id}`, frame);
  });

  const teardown = (): void => {
    conn!.ready = false;
    conn!.ws = null;
    muxConns.delete(wc.id);
  };
  ws.on("close", teardown);
  ws.on("error", teardown);

  return conn;
}

function muxSend(wc: WebContents, frame: MuxClientFrame): void {
  const conn = getMuxConn(wc);
  if (conn.ready && conn.ws && conn.ws.readyState === WebSocket.OPEN) {
    conn.ws.send(JSON.stringify(frame));
  } else {
    conn.pending.push(frame);
  }
}

function registerMuxIpc(): void {
  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:open", (event, handleId: string) => {
    const wc = event.sender;
    getMuxConn(wc).open.add(handleId);
    muxSend(wc, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "open" });
  });

  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:send", (event, handleId: string, data: string) => {
    muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "data", data });
  });

  ipcMain.handle(
    "ao:mux:resize",
    (event, handleId: string, cols: number, rows: number) => {
      muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "resize", cols, rows });
    },
  );

  ipcMain.handle("ao:mux:close", (event, handleId: string) => {
    const conn = muxConns.get(event.sender.id);
    if (conn) conn.open.delete(handleId);
    muxSend(event.sender, { ch: "terminal", id: handleId, type: "close" });
  });
}
```

const api = {
  request: <T = unknown>(req: AoRequest): Promise<AoResponse<T>> =>
    ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:request", req),

  mux: {
    open: (handleId: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:open", handleId),
    send: (handleId: string, data: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:send", handleId, data),
    resize: (handleId: string, cols: number, rows: number): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:resize", handleId, cols, rows),
    close: (handleId: string): Promise<void> =>
      ipcRenderer.invoke("ao:mux:close", handleId),

    // Returns an unsubscribe fn. Main pushes terminal frames on a
    // per-handle channel; we filter to {type:"data"} / {type:"exited"} here.
    onData: (handleId: string, cb: (b64: string) => void): (() => void) => {
      const channel = `ao:mux:msg:${handleId}`;
      const listener = (
        _e: Electron.IpcRendererEvent,
        frame: { type?: string; data?: string },
      ): void => {
        if (frame.type === "data" && typeof frame.data === "string") cb(frame.data);
      };
      ipcRenderer.on(channel, listener);
      return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, listener);
    },

    onExit: (handleId: string, cb: () => void): (() => void) => {
      const channel = `ao:mux:msg:${handleId}`;
      const listener = (
        _e: Electron.IpcRendererEvent,
        frame: { type?: string },
      ): void => {
        if (frame.type === "exited") cb();
      };
      ipcRenderer.on(channel, listener);
      return () => ipcRenderer.removeListener(channel, listener);
    },
  },
};

contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld("ao", api);

export type AoBridge = typeof api;
```

### Notes / caveats
- **System ping/pong:** main ignores non-terminal frames; the daemon also runs ws-level ping/pong under the hood, so the `ws` client responds automatically. No app-level ping is required, but you can add a periodic `{ch:"system",type:"ping"}` if you want belt-and-suspenders liveness.
- **Reconnect:** the relay opens the socket lazily on first `open` and drops it on close/error; it does not auto-reconnect. If the daemon restarts mid-session, the next `open`/`send` will lazily reconnect, but already-open panes won't auto-resubscribe — acceptable for v1, worth a follow-up if you want seamless reconnect.

## v1 implementation (shipped on this branch)

The observe-first slice is built end-to-end:

- **Backend** — `POST /api/v1/sessions/{id}/annotations` formats the captured element into an
  agent instruction and delivers it through the existing `Send` chain (→ zellij paste into the
  agent's pane). Route + spec + 3 controller tests in
  `backend/internal/httpd/controllers/sessions_annotation_test.go`. `runtimeHandleId` is now
  serialized on the session DTO (`metadata`) so the terminal can attach.
- **Electron** — a `WebContentsView` browser (`src/main.ts`), a tiny `browser-preload` + injected
  `browser-overlay` that captures `selector + classes + text` on click, and a `ws`-based `/mux`
  relay for the terminal.
- **Renderer** — `BrowserPane` (URL bar, nav, **Annotate** toggle, bounds-sync) and a real
  xterm `Terminal`, switchable via tabs in `SessionView`. The overlay's capture is POSTed to the
  session via `postAnnotation`.

### Running the demo

```bash
ao start                                   # daemon
ao project add --path ~/Projects/yyork     # register the preview app as a project
( cd ~/Projects/yyork && pnpm web:dev )    # run the preview dev server (note the URL)
( cd frontend && npm install && npm run dev )   # the desktop app
```

In the app: spawn a session on the project → open it → **Browser** tab → type the dev-server URL
→ **Go** → toggle **Annotate** → click an element → type an instruction. On the **Terminal** tab
(or `zellij attach <session>`) the agent receives:

```
[ui-annotation] The user pointed at an element in the live preview (http://localhost:5173/):
  element:  button.btn.primary
  selector: button.btn.primary
  text:     "Save changes"
  request:  make this button red
Locate this element in the code (grep the selector/classes) and address the request above.
```

**Verified headlessly:** the daemon route (controller tests) + the full frontend build &
typecheck. The GUI click + a live agent receiving the message is the step above — it needs a
display and a spawnable agent, so run it in your environment.
